rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The adverbial-genitive construction lacks a cited parallel in this grammatical pattern; Arabic usage also avoids juxtaposing two such clauses without a connector.
rows.anchor: ولم يذكر النحويون في مثل هذا الباب: لو جاء قتلت زيدا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Zamakhshari analyzes the agent of تبين as omitted and supplied by the later clause; Abū Ḥayyān rejects this because deletion conflicts with the proposed subject ellipsis and the Basran account.
rows.anchor: وقد ناقض الزمخشري في قوله: فإنه قال: وفاعل تبين مضمر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: On Ibn ʿAbbās’s reading, the prepositional phrase functions as the passive-subject substitute.
rows.anchor: وأما على قراءة ابن عباس فالجار والمجرور هو المفعول الذي لم يسم فاعله

rows.speaker: ابن السميفع
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sumayfa’s reading has an implicit subject: God made the matter clear to the passerby.
rows.anchor: وأما في قراءة ابن السميفع فهو مضمر: أي: بين له هو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read قال actively and أعلم as a first-person imperfect uttered by the passerby as reflective recognition, like a person amazed by something strange.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: قال، مبنيا للفاعل، على قراءة جمهور السبعة: أعلم، مضارعا

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī glosses أعلم as acquiring direct, witnessed knowledge of what the passerby previously knew only unseen.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي: معناه أعلم هذا الضرب من العلم الذي لم أكن علمته

rows.speaker: أبو رجاء، وحمزة، والكسائي
rows.claim: Their command reading اعلم addresses the passerby, with God or an angel speaking for God as the implied agent.
rows.anchor: وأما على قراءة أبي رجاء، وحمزة، والكسائي اعلم، فعل أمر من علم

rows.speaker: عبد الله والأعمش
rows.claim: Their reading قيل اعلم uses a passive verb whose implicit passive subject is the command itself, not a following clause.
rows.anchor: ويؤيده قراءة عبد الله والأعمش: قيل، اعلم، فبنى: قيل، لما لم يسم فاعله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One grammatical option makes the passerby address himself as a separate addressee, as in Arabic self-address expressions.
rows.anchor: وجوزوا أن يكون الفاعل ضمير المار، ويكون نزل نفسه منزلة المخاطب الأجنبي،

rows.speaker: الجعبي عن أبي بكر
rows.claim: A report from Abū Bakr reads أعلم as a command in form IV; the agent of قال is apparently God, ordering the passerby to tell others what he witnessed, though another parsing allows the passerby as agent.
rows.anchor: وروى الجعبي عن أبي بكر قال: أعلم، أمرا من أعلم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Abraham story follows the passerby story because both demonstrate resurrection by God: the passerby witnesses it in himself and his donkey, while Abraham witnesses it in another.
rows.anchor: كلاهما أتى بها دلالة على البعث المنسوب إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although Abraham lived earlier, his story comes second because the passerby’s amazement, even if reflective rather than denial, lies closer to the Nimrod exchange; if he was an unbeliever, the link is stronger.
rows.anchor: وقدمت آية المار على آية إبراهيم، وإن كان إبراهيم مقدما في الزمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham asks to see the manner of resurrection directly, confirming by sight what he already knew inwardly and had told Nimrod.
rows.anchor: وأما قصة إبراهيم فهي سؤال لكيفية إراءة الإحياء، ليشاهد عيانا ما كان يعلمه بالقلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For إذ, some posit an omitted اذكر and others attach it to ألم تر; Abū Ḥayyān prefers قال in قال أولم تؤمن as its governing verb.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أن العامل في: إذ، قوله قال أولم تؤمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Addressing God as رب gently solicits the request and echoes Abraham’s earlier argument that his Lord gives life and death; the possessive yāʾ is omitted after its kasra and the vocative particle is understood.
rows.anchor: وفي افتتاح السؤال بقوله: رب، حسن استلطاف واستعطاف للسؤال،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أرني is a request of desire; the visual verb takes two objects after the causative hamza, the speaker and the interrogative clause.
rows.anchor: و: أرني، سؤال رغبة، وهو معمول: لقال، والرؤية هنا بصيرية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: كيف تحي الموتى is an accusative interrogative clause; Arabic allows visual رأى and نظر to take such complements.
rows.anchor: فقوله: كيف تحي الموتى في موضع نصب، وتعلق العرب رأى البصرية

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya states that prophets are unanimously protected from major and minor sins involving disgrace; Abū Ḥayyān adopts the broader view that they are protected from all major and minor sins.
rows.anchor: قاله ابن عطية، والذي اخترناه أنهم معصومون من الكبائر والصغائر على الإطلاق،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s request seeks eyewitness knowledge of how scattered bodily parts are reassembled, not correction of a doubtful belief; asking how presupposes certainty that resurrection occurs.
rows.anchor: لأن ذلك سؤال أن يريه عيانا كيفية إحياء الموتى

rows.speaker: الماوردي عن بعض أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The interpretation that Abraham asked how God revives hearts is, in Abū Ḥayyān’s judgment, untenable.
rows.anchor: وأما ما ذكره الماوردي عن بعض أهل المعاني: أن إبراهيم سأل من ربه كيف يحيي القلوب،

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says Abraham saw an animal torn apart by predatory beasts and sea creatures along the shore, prompting his request.
rows.anchor: أحدها: أنه رأى دابة قد توزعتها السباع والحيتان لأنها كانت على حاشية البحر، قاله ابن زيد.

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq attributes the question to reflection on literal and figurative meaning after Nimrod claimed, “I give life and death.”
rows.anchor: أو: الفكر في الحقيقة والمجاز لما قاله نمروذ: أنا أحيي وأميت قاله ابن إسحاق،

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr says the intimate friend of God sought an experience fitting the special intimacy announced to him.
rows.anchor: أو: التجربة للخلة من الله إذ بشر بها، لأن الخليل يدل بما لا يدل غيره، قاله ابن جبير.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In قال أولم تؤمن, قال refers to God and the hamza seeks confirmation: the sense is that Abraham already believed in resurrection.
rows.anchor: الضمير في: قال، عائد على الرب، والهمزة للتقرير،

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says Abraham’s general faith included resurrection and takes the preceding wāw as circumstantial; Abū Ḥayyān finds that grammar unclear because a circumstantial clause needs a governing element.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية. إيمانا مطلقا دخل فيه فعل إحياء الموتى،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The circumstantial-wāw analysis is unclear: the confirmation hamza addresses the full clause containing both the governing verb and circumstantial subject, not the circumstantial clause alone.
rows.anchor: وكون الواو هنا للحال غير واضح، لأنها إذا كانت للحال فلابد أن يكون في موضع نصب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ليطمئن قلبي depends on an omitted clause after لكن, with another omitted clause before it: Abraham affirmed belief but asked to witness the manner for reassurance.
rows.anchor: ولكن سألت مشاهدة الكيفية لإحياء الموتى ليطمئن قلبي

rows.speaker: ابن جبير، وإبراهيم، وقتادة
rows.claim: These authorities explain the request as seeking increased certainty; another reported formulation says Abraham sought increased faith alongside his existing faith.
rows.anchor: وروي عن: ابن جبير، وإبراهيم، وقتادة: ليزداد يقينا،

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says certainty itself cannot increase in parts; the only possible increase is relief from continued thought.
rows.anchor: ولا زيادة في هذا المعنى تمكن إلا السكون عن الفكر، وإلا فاليقين لا يتبعض.

rows.speaker: النصراباذي
rows.claim: Al-Naṣrābādhī reads Abraham’s request as longing to witness the Beloved’s work, then politely explaining the request through reassurance.
rows.anchor: حن الخليل إلى صنع خليله ولم يتهمه في أمره

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī reports a mystical reading: Abraham sought God’s direct address, and hearing “Did you not believe?” itself reassured the lover.
rows.anchor: استجلب خطابا بهذه المقالة، حتى قال له الحق: أو لم تؤمن؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God instructs Abraham to take four birds but does not identify their species; the number may refer to a specified set left unnamed or any four, since naming them adds little knowledge.
rows.anchor: ولم يذكر الله تعالى تعيين الأربعة من أي جنس هي من الطير

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One report from Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the birds as a peacock, vulture, rooster, and crow.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: أخذ طاووسا ونسرا وديكا وغرابا.

rows.speaker: مجاهد، وعكرمة، وعطاء، وابن جريج، وابن زيد
rows.claim: These authorities give the same list as Ibn ʿAbbās except that a dove replaces the vulture.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد، وعكرمة، وعطاء، وابن جريج، وابن زيد: كذلك، إلا أنهم جعلوا حمامة بدل النسر.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report through ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Hubayra names a dove, crane, rooster, and peacock.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس أيضا، فيما روى عبد الرحمن بن هبيرة عنه: أخذ حمامة وكركيا وديكا وطاووسا.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report through al-Ḍaḥḥāk names a peacock, rooster, Indian hen, and goose; another replaces the hen with an ostrich chick.
rows.anchor: وقال في رواية الضحاك: أخذ طاووسا وديكا ودجاجة سندية وأوزة.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Reports from Mujāhid vary between rooster, dove, duck, and peacock, and rooster, dove, duck, and crow.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد فيما روى ليث: ديك وحمامة وبطة وطاووس.

rows.speaker: عطاء الخراساني
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī specifies the four birds’ colors: red rooster, white dove, green duck, and black crow.
rows.anchor: وزاد عطاء الخراساني وصفا في هذه الأربعة فقال: ديك أحمر، وحمامة بيضاء،

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abū ʿAbd Allāh names a peacock, dove, rooster, and hoopoe.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله: طاووس وحمامة وديك وهدهد،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Abraham asked about reviving the plural “dead,” the answer uses four birds, whose referent is itself plural rather than a single example.
rows.anchor: ولما سأل ربه أن يريه كيفية إحياء الموتى، وكان لفظ الموتى جمعا،

rows.speaker: مفسرون غير مسمين
rows.claim: Some interpret four as the four elements in animal and plant bodies, or as birds’ aspiration to rise matching Abraham’s aspiration to the heavenly kingdom; Abū Ḥayyān says the proposed symbolism of the species is unconvincing and the miracle’s wisdom is unknown.
rows.anchor: قيل: وخص هذا العدد بعينه إشارة إلى الأركان الأربعة التي في تركيب أبدان الحيوانات والنباتات،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham is told to hold the birds himself so that seeing and touching together make him more certain of how resurrection occurs.
rows.anchor: وأمره بالأخذ للطيور وهو: إمساكها بيده ليكون أثبت في المعرفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: الطير is a collective noun for non-rational creatures, can be masculine or feminine, and here is masculine; أربعة من الطير is the clearest number construction, while two contrary grammatical rules cited by others are unsound.
rows.anchor: والطير اسم جمع لما لا يعقل، يجوز تذكيره وتأنيثه، وهنا أتى مذكرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent instruction is to place three portions of each bird on every mountain within Abraham’s view, so he can see the parts rejoin when he calls.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه أمر أن يجعل على كل جبل ثلاثة مما يشاهده بصره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read جزءا with a quiescent zāy and hamza; Abū Bakr vocalizes the zāy, and Abū Jaʿfar drops the hamza and doubles zāy by analogy with pause pronunciation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور جزءا بإسكان الزاي وبالهمز، وضم أبو بكر: الزاي،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: اجعل may mean “throw/place,” taking one object with “on every mountain” attached, or “make/turn,” taking two objects with the phrase attached to an omitted element.
rows.anchor: و: اجعل، هنا يحتمل أن تكون بمعنى: ألق، فيتعدى لواحد،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the birds while dead makes the sign greater and makes their return follow Abraham’s call; سعي denotes moving swiftly.
rows.anchor: ثم ادعهن يأتينك سعيا أمره بدعائهن وهن أموات، ليكون أعظم له في الآية،

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl says one does not literally say that a bird “strives”; Abū Ḥayyān treats it figuratively because the birds act like rational beings and rapidly walk, contrary to their normal flight.
rows.anchor: وقال الخليل: لا يقال سعى الطائر، يعني على سبيل المجاز،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stronger parsing makes سعيا a circumstantial verbal noun describing the birds as moving swiftly; alternatives make Abraham the one striving or treat it as an emphatic cognate accusative.
rows.anchor: وانتصاب: سعيا، على أنه مصدر في موضع الحال من ضمير الطيور،

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: A further parsing makes the birds come while Abraham himself goes toward them, meeting them partway.
rows.anchor: وروي عن الخليل: أن المعنى يأتينك وأنت تسعى سعيا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A narrative account says Abraham sacrificed and cut up the birds, mixed their flesh, blood, and feathers into portions on the mountains, called them, and watched their parts reassemble and return headless before calling again; they then came and attached to their heads.
rows.anchor: وروي في قصص الآية أن إبراهيم أخذ هذه الطيور وذكاها وقطعها قطعا صغارا،

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Naḥḥās adds that a headless bird moved away when Abraham pointed with its body and came closer when he pointed with its head, until each met its own head.
rows.anchor: وزاد النحاس: أن إبراهيم: كان إذا أشار إلى واحد منها بغير رأسه تباعد الطائر،

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله
rows.claim: Abū ʿAbd Allāh says Abraham chopped the birds in a mortar, divided the mixture into ten portions on ten mountains, held their beaks, and called them; flesh, feathers, and skin reunited by God’s power.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبد الله: ذبحهن ونحز أجزاءهن في المنحاز، يعني الهاون

rows.speaker: أهل التفسير
rows.claim: Exegetes unanimously say Abraham cut up and mixed the birds’ limbs, meat, feathers, and blood; Abū Muslim rejects this account.
rows.anchor: وأجمع أهل التفسير أن إبراهيم قطع أعضاءها ولحومها وريشها وخلط بعضها ببعص مع دمائها،

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim reads فصرهن as “incline them”: Abraham tamed and trained living birds, set one on each mountain, then called them and they returned; the sign analogically demonstrates souls returning to bodies.
rows.anchor: وأنكر ذلك أبو مسلم، وقال: لما طلب إبراهيم إحياء الميت من الله، أراه مثالا

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim argues that the usual meaning of فصرهن is incline, the text does not say slaughter or cut, إليك conflicts with that reading, and pronouns in “call them” and “they come” refer to the birds, not scattered pieces.
rows.anchor: لأن المشهور في اللغة في: فصرهن، أملهن. وأما التقطيع والذبح، فليس في اللفظ ما يدل عليه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Supporters of cutting appeal to the earlier exegetes’ consensus, say the trained-bird reading offers no distinctive sign, and argue it does not show how God revives the dead.
rows.anchor: واحتج الأول بإجماع المفسرين الذين كانوا قبل أبي مسلم على التقطيع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent wording supports cutting: each of the birds is called a portion and placed on a mountain; Abū Ḥayyān treats that as stronger than Abū Muslim’s objections.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه أجيب بأن ظاهر: ثم اجعل على كل جبل منهن جزأ،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: عزيز means God cannot be resisted in what He wills and implies power; حكيم describes wisdom in His will and representation. Another view calls Him avenger of resurrection-deniers and wise in reassembling decayed bones.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن الله عزيز حكيم عزيز لا يمتنع عليه ما يريد، حكيم فيما يريد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three stories use eloquent question-and-answer dialogue with repeated قال and little coordination: when meaning itself connects successive clauses, an added conjunction is better omitted.
rows.anchor: وقد تضمنت هذه القصص الثلاث، من فصيح المحاورة بذكر: قال، سؤالا وجوابا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: حبة is a generic name for cultivated, edible seed, especially wheat; the poet al-Mutalammis uses حب for grain eaten by a grain beetle. Other forms mean heart’s dark center, vegetable seed, grain, or beloved.
rows.anchor: الحبة: اسم جنس لكل ما يزرعه ابن آدم ويقتاته، وأشهر ذلك البر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: الإنبات means bringing something forth by growth.
rows.anchor: الإنبات: الإخراج على سبيل التولد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says سنبلة is usually analyzed as فنعلة, with nūn augmentative; some linguists attest سنبل, while his colleagues disagree over whether nūn is original.
rows.anchor: السنبلة: معروفة، ووزنها فنعلة، فالنون زائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: من can mean a measure or weight, blessing and favor, or the reproachful reminder of a gift; its underlying sense is cutting off a portion of one’s property for another.
rows.anchor: المن: ما يوزن به، والمن قدر الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: غني is an intensive form of “need-free”; it can also mean residing, while غانية describes a woman whose beauty needs no adornment, as a cited poet says people are each self-sufficient.
rows.anchor: الغني: فعيل للمبالغة من غنى وهو الذي لا حاجة له إلى أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: رئاء is a verbal noun of showing people one’s good deed so they praise and honor the giver, with no other intention.
rows.anchor: الرئاء: فعال مصدر من راء من الرؤية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source defines صفوان as a large smooth stone and records disagreements: some use it as a collective, al-Kisāʾī gives singular/plural analyses, and al-Mubarrad rejects his proposals; Abū Ḥayyān also rejects al-Kisāʾī’s account.
rows.anchor: الصفوان: الحجر الكبير الأملس، وتحريك فائه بالفتح لغة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: تراب also appears as توراب; ترب means becoming poor while أترب means becoming rich, the hamza removing dust/poverty.
rows.anchor: التراب: معروف ويقال فيه توراب، وترب الرجل افتقر، واترب استغنى،

rows.speaker: النضر
rows.claim: Al-Naḍr lists rainfall stages from light رش and طس through drizzle and drops to heavy rain and generous downpour.
rows.anchor: وقال النضر: أول ما يكون المطر رشا، ثم طسا، ثم طلا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: صلد is bare, smooth stone stripped of its dust; other authorities call it a bare surface, a soft stone, or anything devoid of good, and the source notes related usage for slow-boiling pots.
rows.anchor: الصلد: الأجرد الأملس النقي من التراب الذي كان عليه،

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl defines ربوة as elevated, fertile land; the word also has variant forms and a cited poem describes rain over its slopes.
rows.anchor: الربوة: قال الخليل: أرض مرتفعة طيبة،

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash prefers ḍamma in ربوة because the plural الربا is commonly heard; the source rejects al-Suddī’s interpretation as low-lying land and connects the root with increase and height.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش: ويختار الضم في ربوة لأنه لا يكاد يسمع في الجمع إلا الربا،

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Most lexicographers define طل as very light rain; Mujāhid and others extend it metaphorically to dew, and a cited poem mentions dew on a dwelling.
rows.anchor: الطل: المستدق من القطر الخفيف، هذا مشهور اللغة. وقال قوم، منهم مجاهد:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: نخيل is a collective or broken plural like نخل; al-Rāghib derives it from the trees’ selection and notes the date palm’s distinctive pollination and growth.
rows.anchor: النخيل: اسم جمع أو جمع تكسير، كنخل اسم الجنس،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: عنب is a collective name for grapes, with عنبة as its singular; أعناب is its plural and عنباء is another extended form.
rows.anchor: العنب: ثمر الكرم، وهو اسم جنس، واحده عنبة،

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj describes إعصار as a powerful whirlwind that raises dust toward the sky; another view identifies it as a deadly hot wind that compresses clouds.
rows.anchor: الإعصار: ريح شديدة ترتفع فيرتفع معها غبار إلى السماء يسميها العامة الزوبعة، قاله الزجاج،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: احتراق is intransitive, while أحرقت is transitive; حرق ناب can describe a man’s tooth grinding in anger, with a cited line read using either nominative or accusative ناب.
rows.anchor: الاحتراق: معروف وفعله لا يتعدى، ومتعديه رباعي،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the resurrection demonstrations in the passerby and Abraham stories, the passage turns to spending whose benefit will appear at resurrection.
rows.anchor: مناسبة هذه الآية لما قبلها هي أنه لما ذكر قصة المار على قرية وقصة إبراهيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spending passage echoes قرضا حسنا after the Israelites’ death-avoidance story and انفقوا before the Day after David and Goliath; charity presupposes resurrection-belief, and the seed’s seven hundredfold growth demonstrates power to revive the dead.
rows.anchor: فكذلك أعقب هنا ذكر الإحياء والإماتة بذكر النفقة في سبيل الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another coherence reading moves from creation and return to legal duties, beginning with spending and then turning to lawful acquisition; the verse elaborates earlier general commands to spend and supports their reliance on resurrection.
rows.anchor: ويقال: لما ذكر المبدأ والمعاد،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here مثل means description; the comparison may omit “the spender” or “the grower,” or omit both with different implied subjects, as in the earlier disbeliever-and-caller parable.
rows.anchor: والمثل هنا الصفة، ولذلك قال: كمثل حبة أي كصفة حبة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable urges spending on every obedience that benefits Muslims, especially jihad; although some restrict سبيل الله here to jihad, its apparent scope includes required or voluntary spending for oneself or others to support worship.
rows.anchor: وهذا المثل يتضمن التحريض على الإنفاق في سبيل الله جميع ما هو طاعة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spending is likened to cultivation because a planted crop keeps reproducing.
rows.anchor: وشبه الإنفاق بالزرع، لأن الزرع لا ينقطع.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Ḥijāzī readers, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn Dhakwān pronounce the feminine تاء in أنبتت before س; the other readers assimilate it, facilitated by the sounds’ proximity.
rows.anchor: وأظهر تاء التأنيث عند السين: الحرميان، وعاصم، وابن ذكوان، وأدغم الباقون.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seed is credited with growing metaphorically as its cause, though God is the actual grower; one stalk branches into seven, each bearing a hundred grains, picturing the multiplied reward vividly.
rows.anchor: ونسب الإنبات إلى الحبة على سبيل المجاز، إذ كانت سببا للإنبات،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the seven hundred grains can occur in millet and maize, possibly in productive wheat, and the parable remains valid as a supposition even if unseen.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: هو موجود في الدخن والذرة وغيرهما،

rows.speaker: ابن عيسى
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĪsā says the example occurs in millet, while parables may also use what can be imagined without being observed; he supports this with poetic comparisons to mythical ogres.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عيسى: ذلك يتحقق في الدخن، على أن التمثيل يصح بما يتصور،

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says a wheat head may have one hundred grains and other grains more; the chosen figure illustrates jihad spending’s seven-hundredfold reward, beside the general tenfold reward for good works and a sound hadith.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: قد يوجد في سنبل القمح ما فيه مائة حبة،

rows.speaker: مفسرون غير مسمين
rows.claim: Seven is preferred as a culturally salient high number: seven, seventy, and seven hundred recur in Arabic and scripture, while reports describe reward expanding through seven hundred, seven thousand, and beyond counting.
rows.anchor: وقيل: واختص هذا العدد لأن السبع أكثر أعداد العشرة،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī asks why this verse uses the plural سنابل instead of the sound feminine سنبلات as in Joseph, and answers that plural forms may substitute for one another.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: فإن قلت: هلا قيل: سبع سنبلات على حقه من التمييز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects Zamakhsharī’s unrestricted substitution rule: sound plurals mark three to ten only when no other plural exists or when parallel wording favors them.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي قاله الزمخشري ليس على إطلاقه، فنقول: جمع السلامة بالواو والنون،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a word has a sound plural and a broken plural, an established broken plural of abundance, especially on مفاعل, is preferred for counts three to ten; sound plurals are limited or rare according to the other plural’s pattern and usage.
rows.anchor: وتحصل من هذا الذي قررناه أن قوله سبع سنابل جاء على ما تقرر في العربية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: في كل سنبلة may modify سنابل in the genitive or سبع in the accusative; مائة is best parsed as the subject licensed by the preposition, and سنبلة منها is understood.
rows.anchor: وفي كل سنبلة في موضع الصفة: لسنابل، فتكون في موضع جر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A rare reading puts مائة حبة in the accusative, explained by an omitted “produced”; parsing it as a badal fails under the normal categories unless one also supplies omitted حب.
rows.anchor: وقرىء شاذا: مائة حبة، بالنصب، وقدر بأخرجت،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: مائة may mean the ordinary number or simply abundant grain, since Arabs use one hundred hyperbolically.
rows.anchor: وظاهر قوله: مائة حبة العدد المعروف، ويحتمل أن يكون المراد به التكثير،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The example presents farming as one of people’s highest occupations; a sound Muslim report counts crops eaten by humans, animals, or birds as charity, and another report adds what is lost.
rows.anchor: قيل: وفي هذه الآية دلالة على أن اتخاذ الزرع من أعلى الحرف التي يتخذها الناس،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report in al-Tirmidhī urges seeking provision in the hidden places of the earth, interpreted here as farming; a cited poem likewise asks God to bless cultivation.
rows.anchor: وفي الترمذي: «التمسوا الرزق في خبايا الأرض»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Agriculture is a collective duty; if everyone agrees to abandon it, some people may be compelled to perform it.
rows.anchor: والزراعة من فروض الكفاية، فيجبر عليها بعض الناس إذا اتفقوا على تركها.

rows.speaker: مفسرون غير مسمين
rows.claim: Some say multiplication stops at seven hundred; others say God may multiply beyond that.
rows.anchor: والله يضاعف لمن يشاء أي هذا التضعيف إذ لا تضعيف فوق سبعمائة، وقيل:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report attributes multiplication up to two million to Ibn ʿAbbās, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya says its chain is not sound; al-Ḍaḥḥāk says it reaches thousands upon thousands.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس: أن التضعيف ينتهي لمن شاء الله إلى ألفي ألف.

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿUmar says that after this parable was revealed, the Prophet prayed for more reward for his community, then the verse promising patient people reward without measure was revealed; the al-Nasāʾī version also places قرضا حسنا between them.
rows.anchor: وخرج أبو حاتم في صحيحه المسمى (بالتقاسيم والأنواع) عن ابن عمر قال: لما نزلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: لمن يشاء means God multiplies for whom He wills, with an omitted qualification tied to His will; Zamakhsharī says multiplication varies by spenders’ states or exceeds seven hundred for those who merit it, and Abū Ḥayyān flags “merit” as Muʿtazilite insinuation.
rows.anchor: وقوله: لمن يشاء أي: لمن يشاء التضعيف. وفيه دلالة على حذف،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: واسع means abundant in giving and عليم means knowing the intention; another explanation makes God vast in power to recompense and knowledgeable of each expenditure’s measure and reward.
rows.anchor: والله واسع عليم أي: واسع بالعطاء، عليم بالنية.

rows.speaker: مفسرون غير مسمين
rows.claim: Reports connect the verse with ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, or ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf and ʿUthmān; the latter gave four thousand dirhams at Tabūk and kept as much, while ʿUthmān supplied camels, a well, or a thousand dinars according to variants.
rows.anchor: جاء ابن عوف في غزوة تبوك بأربعة آلاف درهم وترك عنده مثلها،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seed parable’s general promise is narrowed: reward belongs to spenders who do not follow their gift with reproach or injury, which nullify charity; seeking praise becomes ostentation, while seeking repayment makes the giver a trader rather than a benefactor.
rows.anchor: لما شبه تعالى صفة المنفق في سبيل الله بزارع الحبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reproach is a grave sin; Muslim reports count the reproachful giver among three whom God will neither regard nor purify, and al-Nasāʾī says a giver who reproaches will not enter Paradise, with two other cases.
rows.anchor: أنه أحد «الثلاثة الذين لا ينظر الله إليهم ولا يزكيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Then after في سبيل الله shows that an otherwise valid gift can be followed by what voids it; acceptance is conditional on avoiding reproach and harm, as the next verse clarifies.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: ثم لا يتبعون بعد قوله: في سبيل الله دلالة على أن النفقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent rule covers reproach or harm by a donor toward a recipient in jihad equipment, other assistance, or ordinary giving, whether donor or recipient fights.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الآية يدل على أن المن والأذى يكونان من المنفق على المنفق عليه

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd limits this verse to people who stay behind and donate, while the preceding verse addresses those who go out with their persons and wealth; thus the conditions differ.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: هي في الذين لا يخرجون إلى الجهاد، بل ينفقون وهم قعود.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Harm is broader than reproach; reproach is named first because donors often commit it, whether by boasting, publicizing the gift, insulting or complaining about the recipient, or forcing acknowledgment.
rows.anchor: والأذى يشمل المن وغيره، ونص على المن وقدم لكثرة وقوعه من المتصدق،

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam advises a donor who fears even a greeting would burden the recipient to refrain from greeting, if seeking God’s favor.
rows.anchor: وقال زيد بن أسلم: إن ظننت أن سلامك يثقل على من أنفقت عليه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An anecdote says a woman asked Abū Usāma for a sincere warrior and mentioned her painful sores; he replied that she had hurt them before giving anything.
rows.anchor: وقالت له: امرأة يا أبا أسامة؟ دلني على رجل يخرج في سبيل الله حقا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reward clause is a predicate of الذين ينفقون; the subject is not construed conditionally, so the explanation continues that this fixed promise does not require a conditional result particle.
rows.anchor: والذين ينفقون مبتدأ والجملة من قوله: لهم أجرهم خبر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reward sentence explains the preceding established promise and therefore states a settled fact without فاء; making it a result clause would imply that entitlement depends on a preceding condition.
rows.anchor: وكان عدم التضمين هنا لأن هذه الجملة مفسرة للجملة قبلها،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another syntax makes الذين ينفقون the predicate of an omitted subject; Abū Ḥayyān rejects taking لهم أجرهم as a circumstantial clause and prefers an independent answer about whether and with whom they have reward.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الذين ينفقون خبر مبتدأ محذوف تقديره: هم الذين ينفقون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ثم reflects the common delay before a hidden motive produces reproach; even reproach accompanying or following a gift has the same ruling as later reproach.
rows.anchor: وعطف: بثم، التي تقتضي المهلة، لأن من أنفق في سبيل الله ظاهرا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Zamakhsharī says ثم marks the superiority of abandoning reproach and harm over giving itself; Abū Ḥayyān says he knows no earlier authority for this recurrent grammatical claim.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: ومعنى: ثم، إظهار التفاوت بين الإنفاق وترك المن والأذى،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ما in ما أنفقوا may be relative with its object omitted or a verbal noun; the phrase also omits “reproach toward the recipient.” Abū Ḥayyān rejects readings that shift “no harm” to the donor or the no-fear promise to worldly poverty.
rows.anchor: و: ما، من ما أنفقوا موصول عائده محذوف، أي: أنفقوه، ويجوز أن تكون مصدرية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A kind reply from the person asked, and forgiveness when a petitioner presses or speaks offensively, are better than charity followed by harm; forgiveness may also be God’s forgiveness or the petitioner’s excuse for refusal.
rows.anchor: أي: رد جميل من المسئول، وعفو من السائل إذا وجد منه ما يثقل على المسئول

rows.speaker: مفسرون غير مسمين
rows.claim: Reported meanings of قول معروف include prayer for the petitioner, consolation and hope in God, praying privately for a fellow believer, commanding right, praise and glorification, concealing one’s own faults, politely encouraging another to give, or a good answer to a petitioner.
rows.anchor: وقيل: قول معروف، هو الدعاء والتأسي والترجئة بما عند الله،

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarīr interprets مغفرة as concealing the needy person’s poverty and poor condition.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المغفرة هنا ستر خلة المحتاج، وسوء حاله. قاله ابن جرير،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reported reading addresses the petitioner, urging restrained, courteous requests and forbidding a display of wealth when not needed; either a kind reply or concealment can benefit more durably than harmful charity.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الخطاب للسائل، وهو حث له على إجمال الطلب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison shares only the general quality of benefit: the benefit of kind speech and forgiveness endures, while the benefit of charity paired with harm disappears; خير may also mean better than nothing.
rows.anchor: واشترك القول المعروف والمغفرة مع الصدقة التي يتبعها أذى في مطلق الخيرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited poet says a gracious refusal is dearer than giving; another says that even without money, a gentle character can offer either generosity or a kind response.
rows.anchor: لا يعدم السائلون الخير من خلقي ... إما نوالي وإما حسن مردود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: قول is an indefinite subject licensed by its description; مغفرة coordinates as a second subject, with an omitted description such as forgiveness from the giver, petitioner, or God.
rows.anchor: وارتفاع: قول، على أنه مبتدأ، وسوغ الابتداء بالنكرة وصفها،

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawī and others parse two clauses, with an omitted predicate after قول: “a kind word is preferable, and forgiveness is better”; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says this loses rhetorical smoothness, and Abū Ḥayyān agrees.
rows.anchor: وقال المهدوي وغيره: هما جملتان، وخبر: قول، محذوف، التقدير: قول معروف أولى ومغفرة خير.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: قول معروف could instead be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning “what is commanded is a kind word”; المن need not be repeated in يتبعها because harm includes it.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون: قول معروف، خبر مبتدأ محذوف تقديره: المأمور به قول معروف،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is غني because He needs no charity and حليم because He delays punishment; another reading stresses that He needs no giver who reproaches or harms and forbears from hastening punishment, carrying warning.
rows.anchor: والله غني حليم أي غني عن الصدقة، حليم بتأخر العقوبة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition repeats because the conditions already stated were not enough: reproach and injury invalidate charity, and the believers’ identity is invoked to strengthen avoidance; invalidation means no reward with God.
rows.anchor: لم يكتف بذلك حتى جعل المن والأذى مبطلا للصدقة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī believes sins do not cancel good deeds; the majority instead say God does not accept charity from someone known to reproach and injure recipients, while another view says the angel is marked not to record it because its intention is not God’s.
rows.anchor: والسدي يعتقد أن السيئات لا تبطل الحسنات، فقال جمهور العلماء:

rows.speaker: القاضي عبد الجبار
rows.claim: Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār argues that the charity already occurred and cannot be undone, so the verse means that later reproach cancels its future reward; Abū Ḥayyān says both readings fit, while the verse repeats warnings to stress the wrong and singles out charity because reproach is especially ugly there.
rows.anchor: وقال القاضي عبد الجبار: معلوم أن الصدقة قد وقعت وتقدمت،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning makes المن injury directed toward the poor recipient, which is the majority view.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قوله: بالمن، معناه على الفقير، وهو قول الجمهور.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says reproach is directed toward God because of the charity, while injury is directed toward the petitioner.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: بالمن على الله تعالى بسبب صدقته، والأذى للسائل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The كاف may modify an omitted verbal noun, “invalidating like the invalidation by the one who spends for show,” or describe the addressees’ state as resembling such a spender.
rows.anchor: و: الكاف، قيل في موضع نعت لمصدر محذوف تقديره إبطالا،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Zamakhsharī takes the spender as a hypocrite who gives for reputation and praise, not God or the afterlife, which he inwardly disbelieves.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا المنافق قولان: أحدهما: أنه المنافق، ولم يذكر الزمخشري غيره

rows.speaker: مفسرون غير مسمين
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies him as an openly unbelieving person who gives only to win public praise; Makkī prefers the hypocrite because ostentation fits someone concealing disbelief.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المراد به الكافر المجاهر، وذلك بإنفاقه لقول الناس: ما أكرمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: رئاء is parsed either as a purpose complement or as a verbal noun functioning circumstantially.
rows.anchor: وانتصاب رئاء على أنه مفعول من أجله، أو مصدر في موضع الحال.

rows.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
rows.claim: Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif reads رياء, replacing the first hamza with yāʾ because of the preceding kasra; this reading is also reported from ʿĀṣim.
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة بن مصرف: رياء بإبدال الهمزة الأولى ياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in فمثله most naturally returns to the nearest antecedent, the ostentatious spender, whether hypocrite or openly boastful unbeliever; another view makes it the reproachful giver and understands two successive comparisons.
rows.anchor: فالظاهر أنه عائد على كالذي ينفق ماله رئاء الناس لقربه منه،

rows.speaker: القاضي عبد الجبار
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Jabbār says the verse first compares reproachful charity to a showy unbeliever and then to dust washed from a bare stone, proving reproach cancels reward after it accrued; Abū Ḥayyān notes this depends on his earlier theory and that the analogy can instead show an initially invalid gift.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي عبد الجبار: ذكر تعالى لكيفية إبطال الصدقة بالمن والأذى مثلين،

rows.speaker: القاضي عبد الجبار وأصحابه
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilite reading treats the rain as reproach and injury removing reward after it was earned; others take the dust as charity already paired with corrupt intent, only apparently attached to the stone.
rows.anchor: وأما التمثيل الثاني فإنه عند عبد الجيار وأصحابه، جعل الوابل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second interpretation is stronger because dust rests visibly on stone without adhering or sinking in; likewise, giving with reproach appears charitable but is not truly so, so the verse can mean preventing either reward or charity from the outset.
rows.anchor: قيل: والحمل عى هذا المعنى أولى، لأن التراب إذا وقع على الصفوان لم يكن ملتصقا به،

rows.speaker: ابن المسيب، والزهري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Musayyib and al-Zuhrī read صفوان with fatḥa on fāʾ; the source calls this irregular in ordinary usage.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن المسيب، والزهري: صفوان بفتح الفاء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: تراب is the subject of an understood “settled upon”; فأصابه coordinates with that verb, its pronoun may refer to the stone or dust, while فتركه refers to the stone.
rows.anchor: وارتفع تراب على الفاعلية، أي: استقر عليه تراب، فأصابه وابل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the image, visible work is dust, the reproachful or hypocritical giver is the stone, and Judgment Day is the rain; on the Muʿtazilite reading, reproach itself is the rain.
rows.anchor: وهذه الجملة جعل فيها العمل الظاهر: كالتراب، والمان المؤذي، أو المنافق كالصفوان،

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffāl offers a seed-store reading: sincere deeds are seed planted in fertile ground and multiplied, while hypocrites sow on bare stone, leaving no crop to retrieve when needed; the analogy therefore implies seed and harvest.
rows.anchor: وقال القفال: وفيه احتمال آخر، وهو أن أعمال العباد ذخائر لهم يوم القيامة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural يقدرون may shift from the addressed believers to a plural sense of the generic كالذي; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says switching back after following the singular form is contrary to the usual Arabic pattern.
rows.anchor: اختلف في الضمير في: يقدرون، فقيل:

rows.speaker: مفسرون غير مسمين
rows.claim: Another view supplies a generic referent: no one can use the seed in dust washed from the bare stone; likewise the reproachful donor, hypocrite, or unbeliever cannot benefit from deeds at Judgment, their intended earnings.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو عائد على معلوم غير مذكور المعنى لا يقدر أحد من الخلق على الانتفاع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling expenditure كسب reflects the donors’ aim to earn; related verses portray deeds performed without God’s approval as scattered dust, windblown ash, or a mirage, and a report describes the first judged as a martyr, scholar, and donor.
rows.anchor: وعبروا عن النفقة بالكسب لأنهم قصدوا بها الكسب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allah’s عدم guidance means He does not guide people persisting in unbelief either out of their disbelief or in their deeds while they remain unbelievers; this favors the interpretation that the parable depicts a disbeliever.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا ترجح لمن قال: إن ضرب المثل عائد على الكافر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fertile-garden parable contrasts the showy unbeliever with sincere spenders; ابتغاء مرضات الله answers رئاء الناس, while تثبيتا answers lack of faith by describing resolve to preserve the gift from corruption, grounded in certainty of the afterlife.
rows.anchor: ذكر ضده بتمثيل محسوس للذهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same three omitted-subject patterns used for the seed parable apply here: the hypocrites may be likened to a planter, their spending to a seed, or spenders and spending together to seed and planter.
rows.anchor: والتقادير الثلاثة التي في قوله: مثل الذين ينفقون أموالهم في سبيل الله كمثل حبة جارية هنا،

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects taking ابتغاء as a purpose-object because it coordinates with تثبيتا, and says spending is not done for تثبيت; Makkī calls both purpose complements, which Abū Ḥayyān also rejects.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ولا يصح أن يكون ابتغاء مفعولا من أجله،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ابتغاء and تثبيتا may be circumstantial nouns or purpose complements; تثبيتا is a transitive verbal noun whose omitted object may be God’s reward, making its acquisition a motive for giving.
rows.anchor: وتثبيت، مصدر: ثبت، وهو متعد، ويحتمل أن يكون المفعول محذوفا

rows.speaker: الشعبي، وقتادة، والسدي، وأبو صالح، وابن زيد
rows.claim: These authorities interpret تثبيتا as certainty: deeply grounded insight strengthens the self to give; Qatāda also explains it as expecting reward, and an anomalous reading تبيينا is cited as support.
rows.anchor: قال الشعبي، وقتادة، والسدي، وأبو صالح، وابن زيد: معناه وتيقنا،
